title: A Town Built on Lava: Fujiyoshida and the Pilgrims' Mountain
standfirst: Fujiyoshida grew on lava flowing from Mount Fuji itself, its streets laid out by pilgrims' lodging-house keepers and its economy later rebuilt on silk. This dossier follows the town from the volcano's dated eruptions through the age of mass pilgrimage, a wartime memorial pagoda and 2013 World Heritage listing, to a 2026 decision about the crowds that listing brought.

sections.heading: A town on the lava flows

paragraphs.text: Fujiyoshida sits directly on the northern apron of Mount Fuji, and its ground is, quite literally, the volcano's own recent history. Research published by Yamanashi Prefecture's Fuji World Heritage Center dates three of the lava flows beneath the modern city with some precision: an eruption of 800–802 sent lava toward what is now the Takamaruo area (a date the same research notes is contested: a 1995 study dated the flow instead to the twelfth or thirteenth century, from a bronze mirror excavated at a site in neighboring Yamanakako village); an eruption of 864–866 produced the Aokigahara flow to the northwest; and an eruption the court chronicles date to 937 produced the first Kenmaruo flow, whose stony, thin-soiled surface underlies the district where Kamiyoshida's oldest pilgrim quarter would later stand. A city planning document lists eight villages — Kamigureji, Ko-Akemi, O-Akemi, Shimoyoshida, Arakura, Kamiyoshida, Matsuyama and Araya — that had taken shape at the foot of these flows by the Edo period, their farmers pushing new fields out onto the Kenmaruo and Hinokimaru-o lava plateaus as population grew. Kamiyoshida itself, the same document states plainly, was "born atop a maruo": a town raised on a lava ridge, not beside one.

One product of that volcanic ground draws pilgrims of its own kind today. Where Fuji's Kenmaruo lava cooled around standing trees, the wood later burned or rotted away and left cave-like hollows in the rock; the largest surviving example, the Yoshida Tainai Jukei in upper Kamiyoshida, is both a nationally designated Natural Monument and one of the twenty-five constituent elements of Mount Fuji's UNESCO World Heritage listing. Local shrine keepers still lead an annual rite there each 29 April, the Tainai-sai, or "Womb Festival", named for the way pilgrims once crawled through the hollow as a symbolic rebirth before their ascent.

sections.heading: The shrine, the mountain and the pilgrim's lodge

paragraphs.text: Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine, at the head of Kamiyoshida's old main street, dates its own founding to a legend of the warrior-prince Yamato Takeru, who is said to have paused at a rise called Otsuka-yama during an eastern campaign traditionally placed in the reign of Emperor Keiko, gazed north at Fuji's slopes, and declared the mountain should be worshipped from that very spot; a torii was raised there, and the shrine's own history dates its formal founding, with a hall enshrining both Yamato Takeru and the mountain goddess Sengen-no-Okami, to the fiftieth year of the same reign. The shrine's own account continues into more verifiable history: after an eruption in 781, the provincial governor of Kai ordered divination, and in 788 a new hall was raised north of Otsuka-yama — the site the shrine still occupies — to which the mountain deity was moved, leaving Yamato Takeru enshrined at the older site.

Ordinary pilgrims came much later than the legend, and in far greater numbers. A Fujiyoshida city planning document dates the widespread popular practice of climbing Mount Fuji for devotion to the second half of the fifteenth century, and it was from this period that the shrine's Great Torii and other facilities of worship, on the mountain and at its foot, began to be developed in earnest. The households that grew rich guiding and lodging these pilgrims were the oshi, literally something like "intermediary priests", and their long, narrow properties still line Kamiyoshida's old street, each with a private lane, called a tatsumichi, running back from the road toward the family's own shrine room. An early-twentieth-century climbers' guide to the Yoshida route already uses the route's modern name without explanation, describing the trail that starts from Kamiyoshida as the "Kitaguchi", the north gate, and noting where it meets the routes from Subashiri near the crater rim by Kusushi Shrine — evidence that the route names familiar today were already fixed well over a century ago. Thirty-eight of the old oshi buildings still stand in Kamiyoshida, the city's own survey records, though only two families continue the oshi trade itself; the rest of the old houses recall it through what visitors still eat: oshi cuisine, once served to lodged pilgrims and, by the city's account, built in the Edo period around dishes such as sliced raw carp.

sections.heading: Silk, noodles and a new kind of town

paragraphs.text: Long before pilgrimage became the town's main trade, the province was already known for cloth. Yamanashi's prefectural government traces the region's weaving back to the Engishiki, a legal code of 967 that records Kai province paying its tribute to the court in woven fabric, and credits later contact with foreign, "nanban", trade goods with helping the local silk called kaiki develop its own reputation. It was in the Edo period that this cottage industry — begun, a Fujiyoshida city document notes, as off-season work to supplement farming — grew into the fine, lightweight weave known across Japan as Gunnai orimono, and by the Taisho and early Showa periods kaiki had become a fashionable lining fabric nationwide; production peaked, the prefecture's own account says, in the Meiji era, and the Fujiyoshida Textile Cooperative, founded in 1951, still organizes weavers in a wider Gunnai textile region whose combined product today makes up some four in ten of Japan's domestically made necktie fabrics.

The mill town fed itself on its own invention. In the early Showa years, the city's cultural-heritage survey records, noodle shops in Kamiyoshida's Kinuya-cho — "Silk House Town" — began serving a thick, chewy wheat noodle to visiting textile wholesalers and workers from the surrounding villages; that dish, Yoshida udon, is still the everyday food most associated with the city. Formal city status followed the textile boom rather than preceding it: Fujiyoshida was created on 20 March 1951 by the merger of the towns of Fuji-Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida and Akemi, gained the Kamiigure district in a further 1960 boundary change, and today, at 121.74 square kilometers, is unusual among Japanese cities in that most of its area — the Kamiyoshida district alone covers over 90 square kilometers — consists of the slope of Mount Fuji itself, reaching the summit within city limits.

sections.heading: A pagoda for the war dead

paragraphs.text: The five-storey tower that now draws visitors above Kamiyoshida was not built as a viewpoint. In August 1958 the city formed a memorial-construction committee under the mayor; ground was broken in April 1959, and after three years of work the tower, modelled on the five-storey pagoda of Shitennoji temple in Osaka and built of steel-plate-roofed reinforced concrete, was completed in April 1962. Rising 19.5 meters — a 13-meter body under a 6.5-meter spire, on a base 7.3 meters square — it holds the memorial tablets of 1,055 people from Fujiyoshida killed in the First Sino-Japanese War, the Russo-Japanese War, the First World War and the Pacific War, raised at a cost of some 9.37 million yen funded substantially by public donation.

The pagoda stands within Arakurayama Sengen Park, reached from the Arakura Fuji Sengen Shrine below by a 398-step flight known as the Sakuya-hime stairway, about 200 meters long; the observation deck beside the pagoda, which frames Fuji and the tower together in the composition now familiar worldwide, was rebuilt and reopened in February 2022.

sections.heading: World Heritage and the four sites in town

paragraphs.text: On 22 June 2013 UNESCO's World Heritage Committee inscribed "Fujisan — Sacred Place and Source of Artistic Inspiration" as Japan's seventeenth World Heritage property, a cultural rather than natural listing built around Mount Fuji's role in belief and art rather than its geology alone. Of the twenty-five separate elements that make up the property, four lie within Fujiyoshida: the mountain itself, so far as it falls in the city; and, in Kamiyoshida, two individual oshi houses kept as historic residences, the former Togawa house and the Osano house, together with the Yoshida Tainai Jukei lava-tree cave described earlier in this dossier. The pairing of an intact pilgrim lodging house with a natural lava feature in the same small listing is itself a statement about how the shrine, the mountain and the volcano's own rock were always treated as a single object of devotion.

sections.heading: Reading the ground today, and its limits

paragraphs.text: Kamiyoshida's old main street still rewards slow walking: the long, narrow oshi plots, the private tatsumichi lanes running back toward household shrine rooms, and the Great Torii closing the view toward the mountain are all still legible, even where a given building has been rebuilt. The lava ridge the town stands on is harder to see directly, but the abrupt, stony rises around the Yoshida Tainai cave and the Kenmaruo district are the same 937 flow the World Heritage Center's own research has dated; comparing them with the smoother, older ground toward Shimoyoshida is one way to feel the different lava flows this dossier's geology has described. The textile trade has left its own reminders in street names such as Kinuya-cho, in the sound of shuttle looms still audible from a handful of working mills, and in the everyday habit of a bowl of Yoshida udon rather than any single surviving factory building.

Success has brought its own problem. On 3 February 2026 Fujiyoshida's city government announced it would not hold its usual spring cherry-blossom festival at Arakurayama Sengen Park — an event that had drawn some 200,000 visitors over its run and more than 10,000 in a single day at its peak — citing overtourism that the city said had begun to include visitors trespassing onto residents' private property, littering, and crowding pavements in ways that endangered local children. The city said it would still post security staff, manage traffic and provide temporary parking and toilets through the expected bloom period in early April, even without a formal festival, with the mayor framing the decision as putting "the living environment and dignity of citizens" ahead of tourism promotion — an explicit attempt, after little more than a decade as a World Heritage backdrop, to choose a slower, more sustainable relationship with the crowds the pagoda's silhouette now attracts worldwide.

timeline.what: An eruption sends lava toward what becomes the Takamaruo area (a date some geologists place instead in the 12th-13th century).
An eruption produces the Aokigahara lava flow northwest of the later town.
An eruption produces the first Kenmaruo lava flow, the ground under Kamiyoshida's pilgrim quarter and the Yoshida Tainai cave.
The Engishiki legal code records Kai province paying tribute to the court in woven cloth, the region's earliest documented textile trade.
Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine dates its founding legend (Yamato Takeru's visit to Otsuka-yama) to this era; the shrine's own account treats the date as tradition.
Following an eruption in 781, the shrine's main hall is rebuilt in 788 on its present site north of Otsuka-yama.
Popular pilgrimage-climbing of Mount Fuji becomes widespread; the Great Torii and other worship facilities at Kitaguchi Hongu develop from this period.
Published climbers' guides to the Yoshida route already use the modern trail names (Kitaguchi) and describe Kamiyoshida's pilgrim infrastructure.
Fujiyoshida City is created by the merger of Fuji-Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida and Akemi towns.
The Fujiyoshida Textile Cooperative is founded, organizing the town's Gunnai-orimono/kaiki weaving industry.
The Chureito memorial pagoda is planned (1958), built (from 1959) and completed (April 1962), commemorating 1,055 Fujiyoshida war dead.
The Kamiigure district is annexed to Fujiyoshida City.
UNESCO inscribes "Fujisan" as a World Heritage cultural property; four constituent elements lie within Fujiyoshida.
The observation deck beside the Chureito pagoda reopens after renovation.
Fujiyoshida City announces it will not hold the Arakurayama Sengen Park cherry-blossom festival, citing overtourism.

caveats: The dating of the pre-Kenmaruo (Takamaruo-area) lava flow is contested even within the source used here (800-802 versus a possible 12th-13th century), and is reported with that uncertainty.

Kitaguchi Hongu Fuji Sengen Shrine's founding date (Emperor Keiko's reign, traditionally around the 2nd century CE) is the shrine's own tradition and is presented as such, not as an independently verified historical fact.

A 1921 guidebook (S2) labels Kamiyoshida "Minamitsuru-gun, Mizuho-mura, Kamiyoshida" (南都留郡瑞穂村上吉田), but this appears to be that book's own error rather than a fact used elsewhere in this dossier: an independent 1919 Minamitsuru county gazetteer (NDL pid 1032181, 南都留郡郷土誌) records named residents of Shimoyoshida and of neighboring Arakura specifically as being "of Mizuho-mura", and Mizuho-mura is recorded elsewhere (Japanese Wikipedia's articles on 瑞穂村 and 下吉田町, used here only as corroboration, since no NDL or official source read this session gives Fuji-Kamiyoshida-machi's own pre-1951 history directly) as formed in 1875 from Shimoyoshida and Arakura alone, renamed Shimoyoshida-machi in 1939, and merged into Fujiyoshida City in 1951 as a town separate from Kamiyoshida's own Fuji-Kamiyoshida-machi.
Visitor and crowding figures for the 2026 cherry-blossom festival decision are those given in the city's own press release; no independent visitor count was checked in this session.
